chapters.label: CHAPTER 01 · GEOGRAPHIC MONUMENT
chapters.heading: A cone that dominates the horizon
chapters.subheading: Its symmetry draws the eye from distant cities
chapters.body: Mount Fuji rises as an active stratovolcano on Honshu. Its summit reaches 3,776.24 m, the highest point in Japan and the second‑highest volcano on any Asian island. It sits roughly 100 km southwest of Tokyo, visible on clear days. Snow cloaks its cone for about five months each year. Five lakes frame its base, offering mirrored views.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 02 · HOLY TRADITION
chapters.heading: A pilgrimage etched in law and legend
chapters.body: Mount Fuji belongs to Japan’s Three Holy Mountains, alongside Tate and Haku. It holds the status of a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and a Historic Site. UNESCO listed it as a Cultural World Heritage Site in 2013, recognizing 25 cultural locations around the cone, including the Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha shrine. An 1872 edict opened the summit to women, ending centuries of exclusion.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 03 · GEOTECTONIC ORIGIN
chapters.heading: A triple junction fuels its fire
chapters.body: Mount Fuji sits atop a triple junction where the Eurasian, North American and Philippine Sea plates meet. The Pacific Plate subducts beneath them, feeding volcanic activity. Its main crater spans 780 m across and descends 240 m. Four volcanic phases built the cone, the most recent erupting from 1707 to 1708. Today the volcano is classified as active with low eruption risk.
